```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# The benchmark needs packages that dtwSat only suggests
benchmark_packages <- c("mgcv", "dtw", "randomForest", "e1071")
has_packages <- all(vapply(benchmark_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, dev = "png", eval = has_packages,
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r , echo = FALSE, eval = !has_packages, results = 'asis'}
cat("**The code of this vignette was not run, because it needs the packages ",
    paste(benchmark_packages, collapse = ", "), ".**\n", sep = "")
```

This vignette compares the classifier of `dtwSat` with three other classifiers, using the example data
that come with the package. It gives an idea of the accuracy and of the processing time of each method,
and of how the processing time is divided between training and prediction. The methods are:

- **TWDTW, GAM patterns**: Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping [@Maus:2016; @Maus:2019] with one temporal pattern
for each land-use class. The patterns are created with Generalized Additive Models (GAM), as in the vignette
"1. Land use mapping using TWDTW-1NN and stars".
- **TWDTW, samples**: TWDTW with all training samples as temporal patterns, i.e. a 1-Nearest Neighbor classifier
without reduction of the samples.
- **DTW, GAM patterns**: Dynamic Time Warping without time weight, calculated with the package
[dtw](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dtw), using the same GAM patterns.
- **Random forest**: the package [randomForest](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=randomForest),
with the values of all bands on all dates as predictors.
- **SVM**: a support vector machine with a radial kernel from the package
[e1071](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=e1071), with the same predictors.

TWDTW is used with the arguments of the first vignette, and the other packages with their default settings.
The example data set is small: 291 training samples of five land-use classes and a data-cube with 999 pixels,
23 images, and six bands. The results below are therefore an illustration and not an assessment of the methods,
see the section "Limitations".

## Data

We read the training samples and the satellite image time series as in the first vignette.

```{r}
library(dtwSat)

samples <- st_read(system.file("mato_grosso_brazil/samples.gpkg", package = "dtwSat"), quiet = TRUE)

tif_files <- dir(system.file("mato_grosso_brazil", package = "dtwSat"), pattern = "\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)
tif_names <- basename(tif_files)
acquisition_date <- as.Date(regmatches(tif_names, regexpr("[0-9]{8}", tif_names)), format = "%Y%m%d")

dc <- read_stars(tif_files,
                 proxy = FALSE,
                 along = list(time = acquisition_date),
                 RasterIO = list(bands = 1:6))
dc <- st_set_dimensions(dc, 3, c("EVI", "NDVI", "RED", "BLUE", "NIR", "MIR"))
dc <- split(dc, c("band"))

bands <- names(dc)
```

`dtwSat` works with the data-cube and the samples. The other methods need the time series as arrays or as tables.
The two functions below get the time series of the samples and of all pixels as an array with the dimensions
time series, time, and band. For random forest and SVM, each time series becomes one row with the values of all
bands on all dates.

```{r}
# Time series of the samples: array with the dimensions sample, time, and band
get_sample_ts <- function(dc, samples) {
  ts <- st_extract(dc, samples)
  sapply(bands, function(band) ts[[band]], simplify = "array")
}

# Time series of all pixels: array with the dimensions pixel, time, and band
get_pixel_ts <- function(dc) {
  sapply(bands, function(band) matrix(dc[[band]], ncol = dim(dc)[["time"]]), simplify = "array")
}

# One row for each time series, with the values of all bands on all dates
as_features <- function(ts) {
  matrix(ts, nrow = dim(ts)[1])
}

sample_ts <- get_sample_ts(dc, samples)
dim(sample_ts)
```

## Methods

Each method has a function to train a model with the samples given by their row number `id`,
and a function to classify time series.

For TWDTW we use `twdtw_knn()` with the arguments of the first vignette, and classify the data-cube with `predict()`.

```{r}
train_twdtw <- function(id, ...) {
  twdtw_knn(x = dc,
            y = samples[id, ],
            ...,
            cycle_length = 'year',
            time_scale = 'day',
            time_weight = c(steepness = 0.1, midpoint = 50))
}

train_twdtw_gam <- function(id) {
  train_twdtw(id, resampling_fun = function(data) mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x), data = data))
}

# Label of each pixel of the data-cube
classify_twdtw <- function(model) {
  as.character(as.vector(predict(model, newdata = dc)$prediction))
}
```

For DTW we take the GAM patterns from the model above and calculate the distance between each time series and each
pattern with `dtw::dtw()`, using its default settings. As TWDTW, it gives a time series the label of the nearest pattern.

```{r}
classify_dtw <- function(model, ts) {
  patterns <- lapply(model$data$observations, function(pattern) as.matrix(as.data.frame(pattern)[bands]))
  nearest <- apply(ts, 1, function(x) {
    # Observations with missing values are not used
    x <- x[complete.cases(x), , drop = FALSE]
    which.min(vapply(patterns, function(pattern) {
      dtw::dtw(x, pattern, distance.only = TRUE)$distance
    }, numeric(1)))
  })
  model$data$label[nearest]
}
```

Random forest and SVM are trained with the table of predictors. They cannot classify a time series with missing values,
so these time series have no label.

```{r}
train_rf <- function(id, ts) {
  randomForest::randomForest(x = as_features(ts), y = factor(samples$label[id]))
}

train_svm <- function(id, ts) {
  e1071::svm(x = as_features(ts), y = factor(samples$label[id]))
}

classify_features <- function(model, ts) {
  features <- as_features(ts)
  complete <- complete.cases(features)
  labels <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(features))
  labels[complete] <- as.character(predict(model, features[complete, , drop = FALSE]))
  labels
}
```

## Accuracy

We assess the accuracy with a 5-fold cross-validation. The samples are divided into five groups, the folds.
Each fold is used once to test a model that was trained with the samples of the other four folds.
The accuracy is the proportion of test samples that get the correct label.

The samples of this data set are pixels of a few fields, and a pixel is similar to its neighbours in the same field.
If the folds are formed at random, most test samples are next to a training sample of the same field,
and the accuracy is too optimistic. We therefore use spatial folds: the samples of each land-use class are divided
into five groups of neighbouring samples, using k-means clustering of their coordinates. The folds are formed
within each class, because most classes are in one part of the area only. Spatial folds that ignore the classes
would leave whole classes without training samples.

```{r}
set.seed(1)

n_folds <- 5
xy <- st_coordinates(samples)

spatial_fold <- integer(nrow(samples))
for (label in unique(samples$label)) {
  id <- which(samples$label == label)
  spatial_fold[id] <- kmeans(xy[id, ], centers = n_folds, nstart = 20)$cluster
}

table(samples$label, spatial_fold)
```

```{r , fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = 'center'}
samples_fold <- samples
samples_fold$fold <- factor(spatial_fold)

ggplot(samples_fold) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = fold, shape = label), size = 2) +
  labs(colour = "Spatial fold", shape = "Land use") +
  theme_minimal()
```

For comparison we also form random folds within each class.

```{r}
random_fold <- integer(nrow(samples))
for (label in unique(samples$label)) {
  id <- which(samples$label == label)
  random_fold[id] <- sample(rep_len(seq_len(n_folds), length(id)))
}
```

`dtwSat` classifies the whole data-cube, so for TWDTW we need the pixel of each sample to get its label from the map.

```{r}
pixel_id <- dc["EVI"][, , , 1, drop = TRUE]
pixel_id[[1]][] <- seq_along(pixel_id[[1]])
sample_pixel <- st_extract(pixel_id, samples)[[1]]
```

The first function below returns the labels that each method gives to the test samples,
and the second function returns the accuracy of each method for each fold.

```{r}
classify_test_samples <- function(train, test) {
  twdtw_gam <- train_twdtw_gam(train)
  twdtw_samples <- train_twdtw(train)
  rf <- train_rf(train, sample_ts[train, , , drop = FALSE])
  svm <- train_svm(train, sample_ts[train, , , drop = FALSE])
  test_ts <- sample_ts[test, , , drop = FALSE]

  data.frame(
    "TWDTW, GAM patterns" = classify_twdtw(twdtw_gam)[sample_pixel[test]],
    "TWDTW, samples"      = classify_twdtw(twdtw_samples)[sample_pixel[test]],
    "DTW, GAM patterns"   = classify_dtw(twdtw_gam, test_ts),
    "Random forest"       = classify_features(rf, test_ts),
    "SVM"                 = classify_features(svm, test_ts),
    check.names = FALSE)
}

cross_validate <- function(fold) {
  sapply(seq_len(n_folds), function(k) {
    test <- which(fold == k)
    labels <- classify_test_samples(train = which(fold != k), test = test)
    colMeans(labels == samples$label[test])
  })
}

accuracy_spatial <- cross_validate(spatial_fold)
accuracy_random <- cross_validate(random_fold)
```

The table has the accuracy in percent. For the spatial folds it has the mean of the five folds,
and the lowest and the highest accuracy of a single fold. For the random folds it has the mean.

```{r}
accuracy_table <- data.frame(
  "Spatial folds, mean" = rowMeans(accuracy_spatial),
  "Lowest"              = apply(accuracy_spatial, 1, min),
  "Highest"             = apply(accuracy_spatial, 1, max),
  "Random folds, mean"  = rowMeans(accuracy_random),
  check.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(100 * accuracy_table, digits = 1)
```

In this example, the three methods that classify with the individual samples have a lower accuracy with spatial folds
than with random folds: TWDTW with samples, random forest, and SVM. With random folds they find a training sample
of the same field next to most test samples. The two methods that use GAM patterns have about the same accuracy
with both kinds of folds, because a pattern summarises all samples of a class.
With spatial folds, the differences between the methods are small compared with the differences between the folds.

## Processing time

To measure the processing time, we train each method with all samples and classify the 999 pixels of the data-cube.
The training time starts with the data-cube and the samples, so for random forest and SVM it includes the time to get
the time series of the samples. In the same way, the prediction time includes the time to get the time series of the pixels.
DTW uses the model of TWDTW with GAM patterns, so the two methods have the same training.

```{r}
all_samples <- seq_len(nrow(samples))

methods <- list(
  "TWDTW, GAM patterns" = list(train = function() train_twdtw_gam(all_samples),
                               classify = function(model) classify_twdtw(model)),
  "TWDTW, samples"      = list(train = function() train_twdtw(all_samples),
                               classify = function(model) classify_twdtw(model)),
  "DTW, GAM patterns"   = list(train = function() train_twdtw_gam(all_samples),
                               classify = function(model) classify_dtw(model, get_pixel_ts(dc))),
  "Random forest"       = list(train = function() train_rf(all_samples, get_sample_ts(dc, samples)),
                               classify = function(model) classify_features(model, get_pixel_ts(dc))),
  "SVM"                 = list(train = function() train_svm(all_samples, get_sample_ts(dc, samples)),
                               classify = function(model) classify_features(model, get_pixel_ts(dc))))

processing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(methods), function(name) {
  training <- system.time(model <- methods[[name]]$train())[["elapsed"]]
  prediction <- system.time(labels <- methods[[name]]$classify(model))[["elapsed"]]
  data.frame(Method = name,
             Training = training,
             Prediction = prediction,
             Total = training + prediction,
             "Share of prediction" = 100 * prediction / (training + prediction),
             "Pixels without label" = sum(is.na(labels)),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
```

The table has the time in seconds, the share of the prediction in the total time in percent, and the number of pixels
that did not get a label.

```{r}
knitr::kable(processing, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0))
```

```{r , fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.align = 'center'}
processing_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(Method = processing$Method, Step = "Training", Seconds = processing$Training),
  data.frame(Method = processing$Method, Step = "Prediction", Seconds = processing$Prediction))
processing_long$Method <- factor(processing_long$Method, levels = rev(processing$Method))
processing_long$Step <- factor(processing_long$Step, levels = c("Training", "Prediction"))

ggplot(processing_long, aes(x = Seconds, y = Method, fill = Step)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Processing time (seconds)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The methods divide their time between training and prediction in different ways:

- TWDTW with GAM patterns spends its time in training, because it fits one GAM for each land-use class and band.
The prediction compares each pixel with only five patterns.
- TWDTW with samples has almost no training, because the model keeps the time series of the samples.
The prediction compares each pixel with all 291 samples.
- DTW has the same training as TWDTW with GAM patterns. Its prediction calls `dtw::dtw()` from R once for each pixel and
pattern, which takes most of its time. This says more about how the function is called than about the algorithm.
- Random forest and SVM spend little time in both steps for a data set of this size.

## Missing values

Nine pixels of the data-cube have a missing value in the blue band of the image of 2011-11-17. TWDTW and DTW do not
need complete time series: they classify these pixels with the remaining 22 observations. Random forest and SVM
need a value for each predictor. Without filling the missing values before the classification,
they cannot give these pixels a label, see the last column of the table above.

## Limitations

- The data set is small and covers one year of a small area. All methods classify most test samples correctly.
- Spatial folds reduce the similarity between test and training samples, but do not remove it: the folds are parts
of the same fields. The accuracy for a new region would be lower for all methods.
- The methods are used without tuning of their settings.
- The processing time was measured once, on the computer that built this vignette. The times are short and vary
from run to run and between computers.
- Cases in which the time weight of TWDTW is expected to matter are not part of this example,
such as crops with a similar shape of the time series in different seasons, or time series with many missing observations.
